title: Mind only
hook: the Yogacara school: how the mind shapes the world it sees

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vasubandhu, who mocked the Mahayana and then wrote for it. Your line was he changed his mind. Which opinion of yours shifted? Day nine hundred sixty-three.

A dream can hold a street, a house, a stranger who speaks, even a fear that makes the heart race. While it lasts, all of it seems solid and outside. Then comes waking, and it was all made by the mind. Vasubandhu, the brother who changed his mind, builds one of his short verse works around exactly this kind of example. He asks: what if waking life is shaped by the mind far more than it seems? Today, the school that asked it.
screen: `A DREAM FEELS SOLID.` → `THEN YOU WAKE.` → `WHAT IF WAKING IS SHAPED TOO?`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tradition explains Yogacara as the practice of yoga, the path of meditators. The school grew from the teachings tradition credits to Asanga and Maitreya, and from Vasubandhu's verses. Its other name is mind only. Second, the dream. In his Twenty Verses, Vasubandhu argues that, as in a dream, places and times and other beings can appear vividly with nothing outside the mind behind them. He adds a stranger picture. Where people see a river of water, he says, hungry ghosts see a river of pus. Same river, different minds, different worlds. Third, the storehouse. Yogacara teachers describe a deep layer of mind, the storehouse consciousness, where every action leaves a seed. When a seed ripens, it shapes how the next moment looks. So the anger of yesterday tints what you see today. Fourth, how to read it. Some readers, in India, Tibet and today, take Yogacara to say there is no world outside the mind at all. Others say it is describing experience: we never meet the world raw, only as our minds have shaped it, and that is what practice works on. Madhyamaka teachers in Tibet debated Yogacara closely, and Tibetan monastic colleges still study both schools. A much older line, from the Dhammapada in Max Müller's translation, points in a similar direction: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." Yogacara takes that thought in its own direction. The mind does not just react to the world. It colors it.
screen: `YOGACARA: THE PATH OF MEDITATORS.` · `A RIVER OF WATER, A RIVER OF PUS.` · `SEEDS IN THE STOREHOUSE.` · `NO WORLD, OR NO RAW WORLD?` · then, large: `THE MIND COLORS IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice your mind coloring one thing. Pick something in front of you, or a person you'll see today. Settle, and breathe. First, notice the color your mind already gives it. Pleasant, annoying, boring, dear. Now ask where that color came from. A memory, a mood, a habit. You don't have to remove it. Just see it as a color laid on top, and look at the thing underneath for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Yogacara. The path of meditators, also called mind only: the school of Asanga and Vasubandhu that looks at how the mind shapes the world it sees. Today's word.
Your line: the mind colors it. Today, when something irritates you, ask once whether the irritation is in the thing, or in the color you brought to it. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Yogacara texts are studied in Tibetan monastic curricula and in East Asian Buddhism, where the Faxiang school carried them, and their account of mind and seeds shapes how teachers in those traditions explain meditation.

fork.setup: you and a hungry ghost stand at the same river. you see water. what does the ghost see, in Vasubandhu's picture?
fork.reveal: same river, different minds, different worlds. Vasubandhu uses it to show how the mind shapes what it meets.

original.note: Sanskrit Yogacara: yoga, practice, and acara, conduct: the path of the meditators.

trapdoor: what you thought: mind only means nothing is real.
what it means: Yogacara looks at how the mind shapes everything it sees, from dreams to rivers to yesterday's anger.
what a scholar hears: Vasubandhu's Twenty Verses, the storehouse consciousness and its seeds, and a long debate over whether it denies an outside world.

notes: Dhammapada 1 quoted from Max Müller (1881); confirm exact wording. It is framed as an older shared line that Yogacara 'takes and goes deeper', not as Yogacara doctrine; confirm the framing is fair to Theravada readers.
'Twenty Verses' is the work's title (Vimshatika); no other count stated. Dream argument and the preta river (Vimshatika 3) paraphrased; confirm.
Storehouse consciousness and seeds (bija) summarized from the Trimshika and Yogacara tradition; confirm.
Two readings (metaphysical idealism vs. phenomenological/epistemic) given without ranking; 'Madhyamaka teachers in Tibet debated Yogacara closely': confirm phrasing.
Yogacara gloss as 'the practice of yoga' and original note (yoga + acara): standard but an etymology; confirm.
howItsDone mentions the Faxiang school; confirm.
The hook's dream is a general illustration.

Editor: 'Yogacara means' now 'tradition explains Yogacara as' (etymology); 'Yogacara takes that and goes deeper' changed to 'in its own direction' so the Dhammapada line is not ranked below Yogacara; 'opens one of his short verse works' softened to 'builds... around', since the dream comes after the opening verse.
Audit: 'both views are still studied side by side' was ambiguous (the two readings, or the two schools?); now says Tibetan monastic colleges still study both schools.
